title: Agents on the Platform: Four Perspectives on the Conversation We're Already Having in Private
tldr: A panel with platform, OpenTelemetry, security and inference perspectives discusses what platform teams must provide to run agents: sandboxing, identity, observability and inference routing. The shared advice is to rely on maturing community projects, treat agents as adversarial, instrument them from within, and learn the stack hands-on before rushing.

key_points.text: Sandbox runtimes are now commodity; build your own only for differentiated needs such as regulated environments or special file system access.
Agent lifecycle raises new ownership questions, such as which identity an agent takes when it resumes after suspension.
Security view: agent workloads should be considered adversarial, and standard containers are not an isolation boundary; use micro VMs without a shared kernel.
For inference, agents are long-running and bursty, so routing must reach the GPU that holds the cached context to avoid paying for uncached tokens.
HTTP 200 does not mean an agent did its job; compare routing guesses (e.g. llm-d prefix routing) with what actually happened, across multiple turns.
External observation is not enough for agents; they need instrumentation from within, like business instrumentation in microservices.
Many agent frameworks now conform to OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, but these are not yet stable because the underlying protocols keep changing.
Tracing has become the default signal for agents, covering tool calls and MCP calls.
Per-agent identity via SPIFFE/SPIRE is preferable to shared service accounts or human identities; egress network policy or proxying is the best value control.
Object capabilities: a proxy outside the micro VM holds the token and performs authentication, so the agent gets granular capabilities and no ambient credential.
Auditing requires tracing delegated authority through sub-agents; context propagation across A2A and MCP is hard to get right.

numbers.text: OpenAI reportedly spent about $1 million on tokens and found around 900 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel.
Running llm-d in production may need two clusters with about 250 GPUs each for redundancy.

open_gaps.text: OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions have no stable release, and stabilizing them on top of fast-changing protocols is difficult.
Container isolation is not secure enough for agents, and sandboxing remains an unsolved cat-and-mouse problem.
SPIFFE/SPIRE gives fine-grained agent identity but has not become common because it is complex to deploy.
Getting started with agentic inference in production is much harder than with predictive inference, given GPU counts and redundancy.

opportunities.text: File issues on agent projects where trace context does not propagate correctly across A2A and MCP calls.
Put a credential-brokering proxy outside the agent sandbox so agents receive scoped capabilities instead of tokens.
Instrument agents from within using OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions and use the traces to drive eval loops.
Pick a pet project that uses agents, tracing and the inference stack (vLLM, llm-d, Ray) end to end.
